definition: To give a false impression of something, especially by hiding or contradicting what is really true.
example: The farmhouse's plain, weathered exterior belied the bright, modern kitchen inside.
nuance: To belie a feeling is to hide or contradict it, while to betray a feeling is to let it show, so the two words are nearly opposites.
prompt: A chess player sits down for the final round of a tournament, secretly terrified.
options: Her steady hands seemed to belie the panic she felt inside.
Her shaking voice did belie her nerves, so everyone in the hall could tell she was scared.
Her opponent tried to belie her by sneering at each of her opening moves.
Her coach will always belie in her talent, whatever the final score.
reasons: Her calm hands hide her fear and give a misleading picture of how she really feels.
The word means masking a truth, not exposing it; "betray" would fit this sentence.
Sneering to make someone feel small is belittling, a look-alike with a different meaning.
This mixes the word up with "believe"; it has nothing to do with trust or faith.

practice.prompt: A shy student presents a science fair project on electrical circuits.
options: He asked his teacher to belie the presentation until next Friday.
His quiet, halting manner tended to belie how much he knew about wiring.
His flawless diagrams belie his expertise and make it obvious to every judge.
A jealous classmate tried to belie the project by calling it babyish and dull.
reasons: Pushing an event back is delaying; the word has nothing to do with scheduling.
His timid delivery made him seem far less expert than he actually was.
Diagrams that display his skill confirm the truth instead of hiding or contradicting it.
Mocking work so it seems trivial is belittling, not creating a false impression.
